passage: Faculty guide's note, project review week. Lakshmi and Pallavi came to me with forty slides for a fifteen-minute talk. Before I said anything, Lakshmi put the deck aside and asked aloud, "What does the panel actually have to decide on Friday? Whether the sensor is ready to be tested in a real field. That is all." Pallavi objected that the survey work would be wasted. Lakshmi replied, "It stays in the report. On stage it only matters if it helps them say yes." Together they rebuilt the talk around one message and kept nine slides. I asked nothing more, but I saw that the talk now had a spine, and both students were calmer than a week ago.

qa.q: How many slides did Lakshmi and Pallavi keep for the talk?
qa.a: They kept nine slides for the talk.

qa.q: What was Pallavi worried about when Lakshmi set the deck aside?
qa.a: Pallavi was worried that the survey work would be wasted, though Lakshmi explained that it would stay in the report.

qa.q: What alternative approach could help if the panel wants to see more data?
qa.a: They could prepare a few backup slides and show them only if asked, because the main talk stays short while the extra evidence is ready.

qa.q: How might a panel member see a talk built on one message?
qa.a: A panel member could find it easier to decide, since the talk answers the question the panel came to settle.

grounding: Students ask what the panel must decide and build a short talk around one message rather than showing all their work.

subtype: Approach: working backward from the audience's need [Thinking]
passage:
Tuesday, 11 p.m.
Final-year project review on Friday. Twelve minutes in front of three professors who decide whether our water-filter project gets lab funding for next semester.
My first draft had 31 slides. Every experiment, every failed prototype, every graph. I was proud of it. Then Ujjwal asked, 'What does the panel actually have to decide?' I stopped. They don't need to know everything we did. They need to decide one thing: is this worth another semester?
So I asked myself: what would convince me, if I were them? That it works, that it's cheap, and what the next step needs. That's it.
I cut it to 11 slides. The six failed prototypes became one slide called 'what we learned'. The opening line is now the answer: 'Our filter removes 90% of bacteria at a cost of 40 rupees, and we need one more semester to test it in villages.'
Scary to delete so much. But it feels right.
– Zeenat

qa.q: How many slides did the first draft have?
How did Zeenat feel about cutting the slides, and what shows it?
qa.a: Zeenat felt scared to delete so much work that had been a source of pride, but settled that the shorter talk feels right.

qa.q: What else could Zeenat do before Friday to check the message lands?
qa.a: Run the eleven slides for a friend and ask what decision they would make, to see whether the message is clear.

qa.q: How might the panel of professors experience the new talk?
qa.a: They get the answer in the first line and the facts they need to decide, which makes their job easier.

grounding: Shows a student asking what a review panel needs to decide and rebuilding the talk around that one message, cutting slides that only show effort.

Kashish: ok thinking out loud. slide 1: 300 students used our bus app in 2 months. slide 2: the problem. slide 3: what we'd do with the space. then demo
Kashish: the building stuff goes in one backup slide in case they ask
Gurpreet: that's a pitch 👍
Kashish: 24 → 7. my heart hurts but ok 😅

qa.q: What does 'my heart hurts but ok' suggest about how Kashish feels?
qa.a: Kashish feels a pang of loss at cutting so much work, but is relieved and convinced that the shorter pitch is what the judges need.

qa.q: What could Kashish do if a judge asks how the app was built?

qa.q: How might the judges see a pitch that opens with 300 users?
